questions.question: On a balmy June afternoon at Lord's in 1983, with India defending a modest 183 against a West Indies side gunning for a third straight World Cup title, this man took a steady running catch over his shoulder to dismiss Vivian Richards. Many regard that catch as the moment the final tilted India's way. Name him.
questions.explanation: Kapil's catch off Madan Lal's bowling is widely seen as the turning point of the 1983 final.

questions.question: He was the first batsman in Test cricket to cross 10,000 runs, the original Little Master, and a Mumbai opener whose 774 runs in his debut series against the West Indies in 1971 still shines on the record books. Name him.

On 10 February 1999 at the Feroz Shah Kotla in Delhi, this Karnataka leg-spinner became only the second bowler in Test history — after Jim Laker — to take all ten wickets in a single innings, dismissing the Pakistanis. Name him.
She captained India to the final of the 2017 ODI Women's World Cup at Lord's, where England won by just nine runs. The most-capped batter in women's ODIs, she is from Hyderabad. Name her.
Bengaluru-born; over thirteen thousand Test runs; nicknamed 'The Wall'. Who?

World T20 final, the Wanderers, September 2007. Pakistan need 13 off the last over to win. India's young captain from Ranchi tosses the ball to medium-pacer Joginder Sharma rather than his strike bowlers. India win by five runs. Who was the captain?
Najafgarh-born opener; first Indian to score a triple century in Tests, against Pakistan at Multan in 2004; nicknamed 'Viru'. Who?

Right-handed batsman, born in Mumbai in 1973, who retired in November 2013 as Test cricket's all-time highest run-scorer with 15,921 runs. His Test debut came at the age of sixteen, in Karachi, against Pakistan.
On 24 February 2010 at Gwalior, against South Africa, this man became the first cricketer in history to score a double century in a One Day International — finishing on 200 not out off 147 balls.
Tamil Nadu off-spinner; master of the carrom ball; over 500 Test wickets and a useful lower-order bat. Initials RA.
Hyderabad-born middle-order batter; nicknamed 'VVS'; his 281 against Australia at Eden Gardens in March 2001, alongside Dravid's 180, is part of cricket folklore.
Bengali southpaw; India's Test captain from 2000 to 2005; widely credited with rebuilding the team after the match-fixing scandal; nicknamed 'Dada'.

On the night of 2 April 2011 at the Wankhede, with India needing 4 to win the World Cup, this player from Ranchi launched Nuwan Kulasekara over long-on for six. India's first ODI World Cup in twenty-eight years.
Born 5 November 1988 in Delhi; took over India's Test captaincy in 2014; led India to a maiden Test series win in Australia in 2018-19; the modern Indian batting talisman.
Punjab off-spinner who, in March 2001 at the Wankhede, took the first hat-trick by an Indian in Test cricket — dismissing Ponting, Gilchrist and Warne in successive deliveries.
Mumbai-born opener and 'Hitman'; captain of India's 2024 T20 World Cup-winning side in Barbados.
Maharashtra-born left-arm fast bowler; opened India's bowling in the 2011 World Cup final; one of the architects of India's reverse-swing era.
He played 200 Tests — more than any other cricketer — finishing his career at the Wankhede in November 2013 against the West Indies. Same Mumbai player as before.
First Indian batsman to hit a century in a T20 international, against South Africa in 2010. UP-born, played for CSK in IPL. First name Suresh.
Indian fast bowler from Ahmedabad with a unique slingshot action; toe-crushing yorkers; ICC Men's Cricketer of the Year 2024.
All-rounder from Moga, Punjab; scored 171 not out off 115 balls against Australia in the 2017 Women's World Cup semi-final at Derby; later India's T20 captain.
Indian wicketkeeper-batter and Karnataka stylist; opener and finisher; replaced Dhoni as India's premier white-ball keeper. Initials KL.
He led India to the inaugural ICC World Test Championship final in 2021 at Southampton, where New Zealand won. Mumbai-born opener (same player as Q16).

Born in Bhopal in 1941; appointed India's Test captain at twenty-one, the youngest in Test history at the time; led India to its first Test series win overseas, in New Zealand in 1967-68. The 'Tiger'.
On 19 September 2007 at Kingsmead, Durban, in a Twenty20 international against England, this Punjab left-hander hit Stuart Broad for six sixes in an over. Name him.

Born Yusuf Khan in Peshawar in 1922, he was given his screen name by Devika Rani when he joined Bombay Talkies. Films like 'Mughal-e-Azam' and 'Devdas' earned him the title 'Tragedy King'. By what stage name did the world know him?
Born in Allahabad in 1942; failed an All India Radio audition in his youth for having an unsuitable voice; that same voice would go on to define an industry. The Big B.
1975. Sholay releases. The film features a dacoit so iconic that his line 'Kitne aadmi the?' is still parodied. The character's name is one word — what is it?
Mehboob Khan's 1957 epic about a peasant woman who refuses to compromise her dignity even as her family falls to ruin; nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Two-word title.
Bengali polymath; directed 'Pather Panchali' (1955), the first film in the Apu Trilogy; won an honorary Oscar in 1992. Calcutta-born.

Mani Ratnam's 1992 film, set against the backdrop of insurgency in Kashmir, broke ground with AR Rahman's debut Hindi-dubbed soundtrack and a young Manisha Koirala. One-word Tamil title also used in the Hindi release.
Delhi-born actor, born 1965, who became the face of the diaspora-romance era of Hindi cinema with films like 'Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge' (1995) and 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' (1998). King Khan.

Aditya Chopra's 1995 directorial debut, in which Raj and Simran's romance plays out across the Swiss Alps and a Punjab mustard field. The film ran continuously at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir cinema for over twenty-five years.

K. Asif's 1960 epic about the doomed romance of Prince Salim and the courtesan Anarkali, made over more than a decade with Dilip Kumar and Madhubala. Released in colour, then re-released colourised in 2004.
Bollywood actress and former Miss World 1994; later won the Padma Shri; now an established Hollywood presence. Initials AR.
Tamil superstar born Shivaji Rao Gaekwad in Bangalore in 1950; once a bus conductor in Bengaluru; his stylised flicks of cigarettes and sunglasses are imitated across South India. Stage name?
Telugu film released in 2015 (Part 1) and 2017 (Part 2), directed by SS Rajamouli; the second film's release inspired the catchphrase 'Why did Kattappa kill...'?
Director of 'Lagaan' (2001), 'Swades' (2004) and 'Jodhaa Akbar' (2008); his films often weave history and music. First name Ashutosh.
Aamir Khan's 2001 film, set in 1893 Champaner, in which villagers play cricket against their British rulers to escape the lagaan. Director?
Born Mumtaz Jehan Begum Dehlavi in Bombay in 1933; her stage name was given by Devika Rani; she starred opposite Dilip Kumar in 'Mughal-e-Azam' as Anarkali. Stage name?
Music director and singer from Madras, born A.S. Dileep Kumar; won two Oscars in 2009 for 'Slumdog Millionaire'. Stage name?

1972 Hindi film by Hrishikesh Mukherjee about a terminally ill young man who chooses cheer over self-pity. Rajesh Khanna in the lead, Amitabh Bachchan in support; the title is also the protagonist's nickname.
Filmmaker brothers from Mumbai whose production house has dominated Hindi cinema since the 1970s — banner now used for 'Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani', 'Brahmastra' and many others. Surname?
1988 Mira Nair film about street children in Bombay, which won the Camera d'Or at Cannes. Two-word title, beginning with 'Salaam'.
1994 Shekhar Kapur film, based on the life of a Chambal Valley dacoit who became a folk legend before being elected to the Lok Sabha. Title is the protagonist's nickname.
Malayalam-language director who has won the National Film Award for Best Director multiple times; films include 'Elippathayam' and 'Mathilukal'. Initials Adoor.
Sanjay Leela Bhansali's 2002 film, a lavish retelling of the Sharat Chandra novel, with Shah Rukh Khan, Madhuri Dixit and Aishwarya Rai. Title shared with the 1955 Bimal Roy classic.
Telugu actor and political icon, founder of the Telugu Desam Party, who served as Andhra Pradesh's Chief Minister three times in the 1980s. Initials NTR.
1979 Hindi film, Salim-Javed's penultimate collaboration, in which a porter at Bombay's docks discovers his roots; Amitabh Bachchan in the title role. Two-word title, character's first name + 'bhai'.
Manmohan Desai's 1977 multi-starrer about three brothers separated at birth and raised in three different faiths — Hindu, Muslim, Christian. Three-name title.
On the night of 14-15 August 1947, this man delivered the 'Tryst with Destiny' speech to the Constituent Assembly in Delhi. India's first Prime Minister.
On 12 March 1930, this man set out from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 followers on a 240-mile march to a coastal village in Gujarat to break the British salt laws. The destination village?
Born Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi in Porbandar in 1869; trained as a barrister in London; assassinated at Birla House on 30 January 1948. Honorific by which the world knew him?
On 13 April 1919, Brigadier Reginald Dyer ordered his troops to fire on a crowd assembled in a walled garden at Amritsar. Hundreds were killed. The garden's name?
The Mughal emperor who built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. He himself was later imprisoned at Agra Fort by his son Aurangzeb.
Mughal emperor who reigned from 1556 to 1605, expanded the empire across the subcontinent, and is remembered for his religious tolerance and the syncretic 'Din-i-Ilahi'. Born Jalal-ud-din.
The Maratha leader, born 1630 at Shivneri Fort, who founded the Maratha Empire and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. Title and name in three words.

She was Rani of Jhansi when the British annexed her kingdom under the Doctrine of Lapse, and led a defence of the city during the 1857 Uprising. She fell in battle near Gwalior in June 1858. Name her.

On 23 March 1931, three young revolutionaries were hanged at Lahore Central Jail by the British, for the killing of an Assistant Superintendent of Police. The most famous of the three was Bhagat Singh; name either of the other two.

Indian National Congress leader who broke with Gandhi over methods, founded the Forward Bloc in 1939, slipped out of British house arrest, and during World War II raised the Indian National Army. Honorific 'Netaji'. Name him.

On 23 June 1757, the East India Company's troops under Robert Clive defeated the forces of Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, decisively. The battle is named after a mango grove on the banks of the Bhagirathi.
On 21 October 1764, Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II together lost a decisive battle to East India Company forces. The town in Bihar that names that battle?
Sultan of Mysore who fought four wars against the British and was killed defending Srirangapatna in May 1799. Tiger-themed throne, mechanical tiger automaton in his palace. Name him.
Bengali poet, novelist and Nobel laureate (1913) for his collection 'Gitanjali'; composed the national anthems of two countries. Born 1861 in Calcutta.
Often called the 'Iron Man of India'; Home Minister and Deputy PM in the first Cabinet; chiefly responsible for the integration of more than 500 princely states into the Indian Union after 1947.
Architect of the Indian Constitution; chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly; first Law Minister of independent India. Mahar by caste, he led the Dalit movement.
Indian National Congress moderate leader who first coined the slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it'; born in Ratnagiri in 1856; the 'Lokmanya'.
On 8 August 1942, the All India Congress Committee at Bombay's Gowalia Tank passed a resolution drafted by Gandhi calling on the British to leave India. Two-word name of the movement.
The 1857 Uprising began with a sepoy mutiny on 10 May 1857 in this town near Delhi, sparked partly by rumours about cartridges greased with cow and pig fat.
On 1 May 1960, Bombay state was split into two linguistic states. Name either of the two new states formed.
First woman Prime Minister of India; daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru; assassinated by her own bodyguards on 31 October 1984 at her residence on Safdarjung Road.
On 18 May 1974, India conducted its first nuclear test at a desert range in Rajasthan. The operation's codename — taking its name from a peaceful festival — was?
Mughal emperor who succeeded Akbar in 1605 and gave his name to a quarter of Lahore; loved Persian art, opium, and his wife Nur Jahan, who effectively ran the empire toward the end of his reign.
Last Mughal emperor; deposed and exiled to Rangoon by the British after the failure of the 1857 Uprising; remembered also as a poet who wrote ghazals under the takhallus 'Zafar'.
First non-Indian Governor-General of independent India (1947-48), and uncle of the man who became Queen Elizabeth's husband. Surname.
The longest river that lies entirely within India, flowing eastwards across the Deccan plateau into the Bay of Bengal. The river that gives its name to the city of Rajahmundry.
Highest peak entirely within India (Kanchenjunga is on the border, so it doesn't count). Located in Uttarakhand, it stands at 7,816 metres. The 'Goddess Peak'.
Indian state with the longest coastline along the Arabian Sea — over 1,600 km. Capital is Gandhinagar.
Largest freshwater lake in India by surface area; located in the Kashmir Valley near Srinagar; famed for shikaras and houseboats.
Capital of Arunachal Pradesh — and arguably the easternmost state capital of India proper.
City on the banks of the Ganga, sometimes called Kashi or Banaras; one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Strait that separates India from Sri Lanka, named after a 17th-century Dutch governor of Ceylon.
Indian island chain in the Bay of Bengal where the indigenous Sentinelese people still live in voluntary isolation. Two-word name of the union territory.
Smallest Indian state by area (since the 1987 reorganisation). Tucked into the northeast, capital Gangtok.
The 'pink city' of India — its old buildings were painted pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales.
Indian state where the famous Loktak floating lake — with its phumdis — is located. Capital Imphal.
The salt marsh of western India, partly in India and partly in Pakistan, that floods seasonally and supports the world's only breeding population of greater flamingos in South Asia. Two-word name.
Indian state created in 2000, carved out of Madhya Pradesh; capital Raipur; rich in coal and iron ore.
The river that originates near Mansarovar in Tibet, flows through Ladakh, and gives its name to a civilisation and to a country.
Indian city famous for its Charminar, biryani, and the Hussain Sagar lake at its heart. Capital of Telangana.
Founded in 1868 by a Parsi entrepreneur in Bombay; now India's largest conglomerate by revenue, with operations from steel to software to salt. Surname of the family.
Founder of Reliance Industries; the man who took the company from a polyester yarn trader to India's largest private enterprise; born in Gujarat in 1932.
Indian IT services giant founded in 1981 in Pune by seven engineers led by N.R. Narayana Murthy; now headquartered in Bengaluru.
India's largest IT services firm by revenue; part of the Tata group; founded in 1968. Three-letter abbreviation.
Founder of the Mahindra & Mahindra automotive group's modern transformation; chairman emeritus; cousin of Anand Mahindra.
The Marwari business family from Pilani, Rajasthan, that built one of India's oldest industrial empires from textiles and cement; founded BITS Pilani.
Indian e-commerce company founded in 2007 by two Bansals (no relation); acquired by Walmart in 2018 for $16 billion.
Indian budget hotel chain founded by Ritesh Agarwal in 2013; the name is an acronym ending in 'On Your Own'.
Indian unified payments interface that enabled instant bank-to-bank transfers via mobile, launched by NPCI in 2016. Three-letter acronym.
Founder of Wipro; transformed the company from a vegetable-oil business into an IT services giant; signed the Giving Pledge.
Banker who, as Chairman of HDFC, oversaw its merger with HDFC Bank in 2023; widely credited with building India's housing finance sector. First name Deepak.
Indian telecommunications and energy conglomerate launched in 2016, that disrupted the mobile data market with free 4G; subsidiary of Reliance.
Cooperative dairy brand from Anand, Gujarat, whose 'utterly butterly' mascot has been a fixture of Indian billboards since 1966.
The 'Milkman of India'; architect of Operation Flood, which made India the world's largest milk producer; founder-chairman of Amul's parent organisation GCMMF.
Indian airline founded in 1932 by JRD Tata as Tata Air Services; nationalised in 1953; re-acquired by the Tata Group in 2022.
Article of the Indian Constitution that abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
The Indian Constitution came into effect on this date in 1950 — celebrated each year as Republic Day.
Lower house of India's Parliament — the directly-elected chamber.
The Indian state that, in 2019, was reorganised under the abrogation of Article 370 into two Union Territories. Erstwhile state name.
Body that conducts elections at all levels in India; a constitutional body headed by a Chief Commissioner.
First woman President of India, who served from 2007 to 2012.
Highest civilian award of the Republic of India.
The Indian Constitution divides legislative subjects into three lists. Name any one of the three.
First Indian Prime Minister to lose a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha; held office for less than a year before losing it in 1979.
The 73rd Constitutional Amendment, passed in 1992, gave constitutional status to which tier of local government?
In the Mahabharata, this Pandava is the eldest brother and the embodiment of dharma; eldest son of Kunti by Yama.
Vishnu's avatar who is the central figure of the Ramayana; prince of Ayodhya; son of Dasharatha.
In the Mahabharata, the charioteer of Arjuna at Kurukshetra, who delivers the Bhagavad Gita to him on the eve of battle.
Elephant-headed deity, son of Shiva and Parvati; remover of obstacles; invoked at the start of any new venture.
Demon king of Lanka in the Ramayana; abducts Sita; defeated by Rama. Name him.
The five-headed serpent on whom Lord Vishnu reclines on the cosmic ocean.
Goddess of learning, music and the arts; consort of Brahma; depicted with a veena.
Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity; consort of Vishnu; worshipped during Diwali.
In the Ramayana, the monkey-god devotee of Rama who leaps across the ocean to find Sita in Lanka.
Brother of Krishna and seventh avatar of Vishnu (in some traditions); known for his strength and his plough as a weapon.

Bharat Ratna playback singer with over six decades of work in Hindi cinema; sang 'Aye Mere Watan Ke Logon' at Delhi's National Stadium in January 1963 in the presence of Nehru, who is said to have wept.
Sitar maestro who introduced Indian classical music to a global audience through his work with Yehudi Menuhin and the Beatles' George Harrison. Father of the singer Norah Jones.
Tabla virtuoso, born in Mumbai in 1951, son of Ustad Allah Rakha. He won three Grammys and was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 2023.
Younger sister of Lata Mangeshkar, also a Bharat Ratna playback singer with songs like 'Piya Tu Ab To Aaja' and 'Dum Maro Dum'.
Pakistani qawwal whose voice carried into Bollywood through 'Tere Bina Jiya Jaye Na' and many others, before his early death in 1997. Initials NFAK.
Carnatic vocalist from Madurai; first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna (1998); known affectionately as 'MS'.
Hindustani vocalist of the Kirana gharana; one of the foremost classical singers of the 20th century; nicknamed 'Bharat Ratna of Pune' before he actually became one in 2008.
Composer who scored the music for 'Sholay', 'Sholay' again, and 'Don'; the 'Pancham' of Hindi film music.
Father of RD Burman, also a music director; composed the haunting 'Mera Sundar Sapna Beet Gaya' and other classics.
Punjabi singer, often the playback voice of romance in 1990s Hindi cinema; 'Tujhe Dekha To Yeh Jaana Sanam' from DDLJ; first name Kumar.
1997 Booker-winning debut novel set in Ayemenem, Kerala, about twins Rahel and Estha; the author's only fiction for nearly two decades after.
Author of 'A Suitable Boy', a 1,349-page novel set in 1950s North India about Mrs Rupa Mehra's hunt for a husband for her daughter Lata.
1981 Booker-winning novel by Salman Rushdie, told by Saleem Sinai, born at the stroke of independence — at midnight on 15 August 1947.
Author of the 'Malgudi Days' stories and 'The Guide'; created the fictional South Indian town of Malgudi.
Bengali novelist whose 'Pather Panchali' was adapted by Satyajit Ray; the Apu Trilogy is based on his work.
Trinidad-born writer of Indian descent; won the Booker for 'In a Free State' (1971) and the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2001. Surname.
Author of 'The White Tiger' (Booker 2008) and 'Selection Day'; set his Booker novel as a letter from Balram Halwai to the Chinese premier.
Bengali polymath whose play 'Dak Ghar' (The Post Office) and song collections 'Gitanjali' (which won him the Nobel) shaped modern Indian literature.
Author of 'Train to Pakistan', 'I Shall Not Hear the Nightingale' and a long-running newspaper column; lived in Kasauli; died in 2014 at the age of 99.
Author of 'The Shadow Lines' and 'The Hungry Tide'; his 'Ibis Trilogy' opens with 'Sea of Poppies'. Calcutta-born.
Indian space agency that successfully landed Chandrayaan-3 near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023.
Indian-American astronaut, born in Karnal, Haryana, who died in the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster on 1 February 2003.
Indian mathematician, born 1887 in Erode, who travelled to Cambridge to work with G.H. Hardy and made startling contributions to number theory before dying at 32.
Indian-origin chess Grandmaster who became World Champion in December 2024 at the age of 18, the youngest ever to do so. Initials D.G.
Indian boxer from Manipur; six-time World Amateur Champion; Olympic bronze medallist at London 2012; Rajya Sabha MP. Goes by the nickname 'Magnificent Mary'.

He was Champion of Champions at the 1985 Benson & Hedges World Championship of Cricket in Melbourne, where India beat Pakistan in the final. The Audi car he won — driving it around the MCG with team-mates clinging on — became one of the iconic images of Indian cricket. Bombay all-rounder, later India coach.

Man of the Match in both the semi-final and the final of the 1983 World Cup; took 3 for 12 against the West Indies at Lord's. Punjab-born medium-pacer and middle-order batter; son of one Test cricketer, brother of another.

On 12 December 2003 at the MCG, this Indian opener struck 195 in the second innings — at the time the highest individual Test score by an Indian on Australian soil. Najafgarh man, but a different innings to the one we've already heard about.

He took the boundary catch — juggled, stepped over the rope, then stepped back in to complete the dismissal of David Miller — in the final over of the 2024 T20 World Cup final at Bridgetown. Mumbai-born middle-order batter, T20 specialist, nicknamed 'SKY'.

Bengali director, contemporary of Satyajit Ray and Mrinal Sen; films 'Meghe Dhaka Tara' (1960) and 'Subarnarekha' are part of his Partition trilogy. He died young, in 1976, his work largely under-recognised in his lifetime.

1959 Guru Dutt film, considered by many his masterpiece; tells the story of a film director whose unfortunate timing means he is celebrated only after his death. Flopped on release; today regularly listed among the greatest Indian films ever made.
M.S. Sathyu's 1973 art-house film, set during Partition, about a Muslim shoemaker family in Agra torn between staying in India and leaving for Pakistan. Title is two Urdu words meaning 'hot winds'.
On 4 February 1922, a mob of Non-Cooperation protesters at this UP village set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi promptly suspended the entire Non-Cooperation Movement.

He founded the Hindustan Republican Association in 1924, was a key planner of the Kakori train robbery in August 1925, and was hanged at Gorakhpur Jail on 19 December 1927. His Urdu ghazal 'Sarfaroshi ki Tamanna' became a revolutionary anthem.
Retired British civil servant and ornithologist who was the prime mover behind the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885, and served as its first General Secretary. Surname.
19th-century Bengali polymath; fierce campaigner for widow remarriage in Hindu society; his Sanskrit reforms and primer 'Borno Porichoy' shaped Bengali education for generations.
Bengali reformer of the early 19th century; founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828; campaigned successfully against sati; honoured with the title 'Raja' by the Mughal emperor though he was not royalty.
Highest peak in South India, in Tamil Nadu's Nilgiri district, at 2,637 metres. The name in Kannada means 'big peak'.
Southernmost tip of Indian territory, on Great Nicobar Island, named after a Prime Minister.
Indian-American CEO of Microsoft from 2014; born in Hyderabad in 1967; alumnus of Manipal Institute of Technology and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee.
Indian-origin CEO of Alphabet (Google's parent) since 2019, after running Google itself from 2015; born in Madurai in 1972; alumnus of IIT Kharagpur and Stanford.
He coined the term 'Hindutva' in his 1923 essay of that name, written while imprisoned in the Andaman Cellular Jail; later President of the Hindu Mahasabha.

In the Mahabharata, the great-grandfather of the Pandavas — son of King Shantanu and the goddess Ganga — who is granted the boon of choosing his own time of death, and finally falls on a bed of arrows at Kurukshetra.

Asura king who, through severe penance, wins from Brahma a boon of near-immortality — cannot be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors. Vishnu finally slays him as Narasimha, on a threshold, at twilight.
Sarod maestro who founded the Maihar gharana of Hindustani classical music; teacher of Pandit Ravi Shankar and Ustad Ali Akbar Khan (his son). Born in 1862, lived past 100.
Bengali polymath who composed the song 'Vande Mataram', taken from his 1882 novel 'Anandamath'.
Author of 'The Discovery of India', written largely in jail at Ahmednagar Fort between 1942 and 1946. Allahabad-born politician we've met before.
Tamil novelist who serialised 'Ponniyin Selvan' in the magazine Kalki from 1950 to 1954 — the historical epic about the Cholas, adapted by Mani Ratnam in 2022. Pen name shared with the magazine.
Booker Prize winner 2006 for 'The Inheritance of Loss', set in Kalimpong against the backdrop of the Gorkhaland movement. Daughter of the novelist Anita Desai.
First Indian to win an individual Olympic gold medal — at Beijing 2008, in the men's 10m air rifle. From Chandigarh.
Five-time World Chess Champion (between 2000 and 2013); a Padma Vibhushan; nicknamed 'Vishy' or 'the Madras Tiger'.
Right-arm medium-pacer who took 3 for 31 in the 1983 World Cup final at Lord's, dismissing both Greenidge and Vivian Richards. Delhi-born; later India coach.
Karnataka all-rounder who took the most wickets — 18 — at the 1983 Prudential World Cup, more than any other bowler in the tournament. Often overshadowed by his more famous team-mates.
Maharashtra batter who scored a blazing 174 against England at Old Trafford in 1982, including a sequence of six fours in an over off Bob Willis. Later, MP from Solapur for Shiv Sena.
Hyderabad-born middle-order batter; scored hundreds in each of his first three Test innings against England in 1984-85; captained India in 47 Tests; banned for life in 2000 over match-fixing.
Mumbai opener who, alongside Gavaskar, formed one of Indian cricket's iconic opening pairs. He top-scored with 38 in the 1983 World Cup final at Lord's. Initials K.S.
Mumbai-born middle-order batter who scored three Test centuries at Lord's — in 1979, 1982 and 1986. The 'Colonel'.
Karnataka fast bowler with a textbook action; 236 Test wickets, the most by any Indian fast bowler at the time of his retirement in 2002. Initials J.S.
Mumbai-born medium-pacer and lower-order batter; fastest Indian to 50 ODI wickets at the time; later chairman of selectors from 2023.
Maharashtra-born left-handed opener; the cornerstone of the Indian women's batting lineup in the 2010s and 2020s; ICC Women's Cricketer of the Year 2018 and 2021.
Bengal-born right-arm medium pacer; the most prolific wicket-taker in women's ODIs ever, with over 250 wickets. Padma Shri.
Karnataka leg-spinner whose right arm was withered by polio in childhood; he went on to take 242 Test wickets between 1964 and 1979, often spearheading India's famous spin quartet. Initials B.S.
Punjab-born left-arm orthodox spinner; one of India's famous spin quartet of the 1960s and 70s, alongside Chandra, Prasanna and Venkat; captained India in 22 Tests.
Mumbai all-rounder; scored 231 against New Zealand at Madras in February 1956 — the first Test double century by an Indian. He's also remembered as the man who gave 'Mankading' its name.
He led India in their inaugural Test match — at Lord's in June 1932, against England. The first Indian Test captain. Nagpur-born.
Bengal opener whose 413-run partnership with Vinoo Mankad against New Zealand at Madras in 1956 stood as a Test world record opening stand for over fifty years.

Mumbai right-hander, twelve Test centuries, India captain in eight Tests in the 1950s; also the man who hit Frank Tyson for the only six in the 1955 Madras Test. Affectionately, the 'Palm Tree Hitter'.
Bombay leg-spinner of the 1950s; 9 for 102 against the West Indies at Kanpur in 1958-59 — the only nine-wicket haul by an Indian in Tests until Kumble's ten in 1999.
Hyderabadi stylist of the 1960s; played 39 Tests; brother-in-law of MAK Pataudi. Initials M.L.
India's premier first-class domestic trophy, established in 1934-35 and named after the prince of Nawanagar (1872-1933) who became one of the great batsmen of his era at Sussex and England.
Karnataka-born off-spinner of the famous quartet; took 189 Test wickets between 1962 and 1978; surname begins with 'P'.
Madhya Pradesh-born actor (1935-); the 'He-Man' of Bollywood; Veeru in 'Sholay'; husband of Hema Malini; later a BJP MP from Bikaner.
Bengali actor who played the adult Apu in Ray's 'Apur Sansar' (1959), and went on to be Ray's most frequent collaborator across 14 films.
Tamil actor who founded the AIADMK in 1972; Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu three times in the late 70s and 80s; introduced the mid-day meal scheme. Three letters by which he is known.
He directed 'Sholay' (1975) — the most-watched Hindi film of its era — bringing to life the Salim-Javed screenplay. Mumbai filmmaker; later directed 'Shaan' and 'Saagar'.
Director of 'Neecha Nagar' (1946), the only Indian film ever to win the top prize at Cannes (then the Grand Prize, predecessor to the Palme d'Or). Brother of Dev and Vijay.
Tamil-born Bollywood actress, the 'Dream Girl' after her 1977 film of that name; opposite Dharmendra in many films and later his wife; also a Bharatanatyam dancer and BJP MP.
Anglo-Burmese dancer-actor who became the most famous cabaret performer in Hindi cinema; songs include 'Piya Tu Ab To Aaja' and 'Mehbooba Mehbooba'. Single name.
Mumbai-born actress; her 'Dhak Dhak' number from 'Beta' (1992) is iconic; films include 'Tezaab', 'Hum Aapke Hain Koun', 'Devdas'. Padma Shri 2008.
Indian-American director of 'Salaam Bombay!' (1988), 'Mississippi Masala' (1991), and 'Monsoon Wedding' (2001), which won the Golden Lion at Venice. Surname?
Director of 'Deewaar' (1975), 'Kabhi Kabhie' (1976), 'Silsila' (1981) and 'Veer-Zaara' (2004); founder of Yash Raj Films.
Punjab-born actor of parallel cinema; films 'Aakrosh' (1980), 'Ardh Satya' (1983), 'Mirch Masala' (1987), 'Maachis' (1996); also crossed over to Hollywood and British cinema.
Maharashtra-born actress, considered the bridge between parallel cinema and the mainstream; 'Bhumika' (1977), 'Manthan' (1976), 'Arth' (1982). Died in December 1986 at the age of 31.
Bengali director, contemporary of Ray and Ghatak; his 'Bhuvan Shome' (1969), about a stiff bureaucrat softened by a village girl, is widely seen as the start of Indian parallel cinema.
Adoor Gopalakrishnan's 1981 Malayalam film about a feudal landlord trapped in his own decaying mansion, slowly losing his hold on reality. Title means 'rat-trap'.
1937 Marathi devotional film by V. Shantaram; the first Indian sound film to be screened at an international film festival, in Venice. Title is the name of a 17th-century saint-poet.
Bimal Roy's 1953 film about a peasant who loses his land to a moneylender and migrates to Calcutta to work as a rickshaw-puller. Title literally means 'two acres of land'.

1957 Guru Dutt film, often paired with 'Kaagaz Ke Phool' as his masterpiece; about a poet, Vijay, struggling for recognition in a hostile society. The Sahir Ludhianvi-Burman soundtrack alone — 'Yeh Duniya Agar Mil Bhi Jaaye To Kya Hai' — is a classic. Hindi title means 'thirsty'.
Satyajit Ray's 1963 film, set in 1950s Calcutta, about a housewife who becomes a working woman to support her family. Title is the Bengali word for 'big city'.
UP-born actor, FTII alumnus; National Film Award for Best Actor three times — for 'Sparsh' (1979), 'Paar' (1984) and 'Iqbal' (2005); also a celebrated stage actor.
Telangana-born director, the leading figure of Indian parallel cinema in the 70s and 80s; films include 'Ankur' (1974), 'Manthan' (1976), 'Bhumika' (1977), 'Mandi' (1983).
Three battles, three centuries, one Haryana town: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi here in 1526, the Mughals defeated Hemu here in 1556, and Abdali defeated the Marathas here in 1761. The town?
Tenth and last human Guru of Sikhism; founded the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi 1699; declared the Guru Granth Sahib his eternal successor in 1708.
Founder of Sikhism, born around 1469 at Talwandi (now in Pakistan); the first Sikh Guru.
Founder of the Sikh Empire (1799-1839) with its capital at Lahore; one-eyed; called the 'Lion of Punjab'; claimant of the Koh-i-Noor in his lifetime.
She presided over the 1925 Kanpur session of the Indian National Congress, becoming the first Indian woman to be Congress president. Poet too — 'Nightingale of India'.
First Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons, in 1892, on a Liberal ticket from Finsbury Central; nicknamed the 'Grand Old Man of India'; mentor to Gokhale, Tilak and Gandhi.

Bharatiya Janata Party founder; lawyer and President of the All India Trinamool Congress... wait, mixed it up. Let me try again. He led the Khilafat Movement (1919-22) along with his elder brother Shaukat Ali. Indian Muslim leader and journalist. Honorific 'Maulana'.
He founded Banaras Hindu University in 1916 with the support of the British Crown after years of fundraising across princely states; later President of the INC; honorific 'Mahamana'.
Punjabi nationalist leader, the 'Lion of Punjab' (Punjab Kesari); died in November 1928 of injuries sustained from a police lathi-charge during protests against the Simon Commission in Lahore.
Bengali revolutionary; 'Master Da'; led the Chittagong armoury raid on 18 April 1930, an attempt to seize British arms in the Chittagong arsenal. Hanged in 1934.
Maratha queen who, after her husband's death, ruled the kingdom of Indore from 1767 to 1795; renowned for her piety, temple-building and just governance. Initials A.H.
Irish-British theosophist who became Indian National Congress president in 1917, the first woman to do so; founder of the Home Rule League with Tilak.
On 13 March 1940, this Punjabi revolutionary shot dead Michael O'Dwyer at Caxton Hall in London — the British official who had endorsed the Jallianwala Bagh massacre 21 years earlier.

Bengali nationalist who founded the revolutionary group Anushilan Samiti in 1902, was tried for the Alipore bomb case (1908), and later renounced politics for spiritual life at Pondicherry, where he founded an ashram.

Tribal leader of the Mundas; led an uprising against British and missionary encroachment in Chota Nagpur (now Jharkhand) in 1899-1900; died in jail at Ranchi in June 1900 at age 25; called 'Bhagwan' by his followers.
Begum of Awadh; led the rebel forces in Lucknow during the 1857 Uprising while her husband Wajid Ali Shah was in British exile in Calcutta; later fled to Nepal.
Persian invader who, in 1739, defeated Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal, sacked Delhi, and carried the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond back to Persia.
Afghan ruler who defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat on 14 January 1761, halting Maratha expansion. Founder of the Durrani Empire.
Two brothers founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336, declaring independence from the Delhi Sultanate and establishing a capital at Hampi. Name either.

Bengali revolutionary who threw bombs at the Imperial Legislative Assembly in Delhi on 8 April 1929 alongside Bhagat Singh; both surrendered to be tried; he survived prison and died in 1965. Initials B.K.
First female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; daughter of Iltutmish; reigned from 1236 to 1240 before being deposed by the nobles. The film Hema Malini played her in 1983.
Father of Tipu Sultan; the de facto ruler of Mysore from 1761; modernised the Mysore army with French help; fought the First and Second Anglo-Mysore Wars.
Sufi saint of the Chishti order, based in Delhi; lived 1238-1325; spiritual mentor of Amir Khusrau; his dargah remains a pilgrimage site for all faiths.
Bengali statistician and physicist who founded the Indian Statistical Institute at Calcutta in 1931; lent his name to a measure of distance still used in multivariate statistics. Initials P.C.
First Education Minister of independent India (1947-58); a leader of the Khilafat Movement before independence; the man whose birthday (11 November) is celebrated as National Education Day.
Mighty river that originates as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, enters India through Arunachal Pradesh, and forms the great delta with the Ganga before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
Mountain range that runs roughly parallel to India's west coast for about 1,600 km, from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu; one of the world's eight 'hottest hotspots' of biological diversity.
Hill town and tea-growing centre in West Bengal; toy train; views of Kanchenjunga.
Northeastern Indian state, capital Kohima; site of one of the most decisive World War II battles, where Indian and British troops halted the Japanese advance in 1944.
Southernmost mainland point of India; in Tamil Nadu; the meeting place of the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean. The Vivekananda Rock Memorial sits offshore.
Mangrove forest in the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta, shared between India and Bangladesh; home of the Royal Bengal tiger.
Indian Union Territory carved out of Goa, Daman and Diu in 2020 — wait, the other way: the UT formed by merging Daman and Diu with Dadra and Nagar Haveli in 2020.
