questions.question: Highest peak in the Western Ghats, located in Kerala's Idukki district at 2,695 metres. The name in Malayalam means 'elephant peak'.
Highest point of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, at 732 metres on North Andaman Island.
Indian high-altitude pass, at 4,170 metres, between Tawang and Bomdila in Arunachal Pradesh; site of fierce fighting in the 1962 war with China.
Longest lake in India, in Kerala; an expanded estuary that runs parallel to the Arabian Sea behind the coastal sandbar; 96 km long; gives Alappuzha its houseboat tourism.
Maharashtra crater lake, in Buldhana district; formed by a meteor impact roughly 50,000 years ago in basaltic rock — geologically rare.
Indian state where the Living Root Bridges of the Khasi and Jaintia people are found; capital Shillong.
Indian high-altitude pass, in Sikkim's Himalayan range, that connects to Tibet; reopened for limited border trade with China in 2006.
Capital of the Indian Union Territory of Lakshadweep — also the name of one of its inhabited islands.

Eldest son of Dhirubhai Ambani; chairman of Reliance Industries since his father's death in 2002; took control of the petrochemicals, refining, telecom and retail businesses after splitting with his younger brother in 2005.
Chairman of the Mahindra Group since 2012; grandson of one of the founders; Harvard MBA; well-known for thoughtful tweets and championing Indian manufacturing.
Indian-American business executive; CEO of PepsiCo from 2006 to 2018; born and raised in Chennai; alumna of IIM Calcutta and Yale.
Rajasthan-born steel magnate; chairman of ArcelorMittal; one-time richest Indian and richest Asian in the UK.
Founder of the Future Group; the man who pioneered the Indian organised retail story with Big Bazaar and Pantaloons in the 2000s; later filed for bankruptcy.
Founded Jet Airways in 1993; once India's largest private airline. The carrier collapsed in April 2019; he later faced legal troubles in Britain.
Mangalore-born business tycoon who founded Kingfisher Airlines and ran the United Breweries Group; declared a fugitive economic offender in 2019; resident in the UK.
Mysore-born co-founder and former chairman of Infosys; came up with the line 'powered by intellect, driven by values'; husband of Sudha Murthy, father-in-law of UK's Rishi Sunak.

Chaired the Tata Group from 1991 to 2012, and again briefly in 2016-17; oversaw the acquisitions of Tetley (2000), Corus (2007) and Jaguar Land Rover (2008); ran the Tata Trusts. Bharat Ratna 2024 (posthumous-ish) — actually awarded shortly before his death; died October 2024.
First Indian to receive a commercial pilot's licence (1929); chaired the Tata Group for 50 years (1938-91); founded Tata Air Services in 1932, India's first airline. Bharat Ratna 1992.

Marwari businessman from Pilani who built one of India's earliest industrial empires from textiles, cement and aluminium; close associate of Gandhi; the Birla House (now Gandhi Smriti) in Delhi was his residence.
Pune-born industrialist of the early 20th century; founded Hindustan Aircraft (now HAL) and Premier Automobiles; pioneer of Indian shipbuilding too. Surname?
Bangalore-based entrepreneur; founded Biocon in 1978 from a garage with seed capital of ten thousand rupees; today one of India's leading biopharmaceutical figures.
Mumbai-born entrepreneur; was an investment banker with Kotak Mahindra; founded Nykaa in 2012 at the age of 50; rang the bell when the company listed on the BSE in 2021.
IIT Bombay alumnus; co-founded Ola Cabs in 2010 and later Ola Electric; both companies disrupted Indian transport sectors.
Second President of India (1962-67) and a philosopher of Hinduism; his birthday, 5 September, is celebrated as Teachers' Day.
11th President of India (2002-07); aerospace scientist who led the development of India's first SLV-3 and later directed the IGMDP missile programme; the 'People's President'.
First Dalit President of India (1997-2002); a Kerala-born diplomat-turned-politician who served as ambassador to Thailand, China and the US.
Economist; Finance Minister 1991-96; PM 2004-2014; widely credited as the architect of India's 1991 economic liberalisation. Born in pre-Partition Punjab in 1932.
BJP leader; Prime Minister of India three times — for 13 days in 1996, then 1998-99, then 1999-2004; Hindi poet; signed the Lahore Bus declaration with Nawaz Sharif in 1999.
Bihar-born; first President of India (1950-62); served two consecutive terms; before that, the President of the Constituent Assembly of India that drafted the Constitution.
Constitutional adviser to the Constituent Assembly of India; prepared the initial draft of what became the Indian Constitution; later judge of the International Court of Justice. Initials B.N.
Tamil Nadu-born civil servant; Chief Election Commissioner of India from 1990 to 1996; transformed the conduct of Indian elections by enforcing the Model Code of Conduct and curbing booth capturing.
Andhra-born Congress leader; Prime Minister 1991-96; appointed Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister and oversaw the dismantling of the licence-permit raj.
He served as the fifth Prime Minister of India for less than six months in 1979-80, never having to face Parliament after his appointment. Jat leader from western UP.
Trinity-of-three: Brahma the creator, Shiva the destroyer, and the third — preserver of the universe — who incarnates as Rama, Krishna and Buddha (per some traditions). Name him.
The destroyer in the Hindu trinity; lord of the cosmic dance; abode at Mount Kailash; consort Parvati.
Wife of Shiva; mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya; daughter of Himavan, king of the Himalayas. Also worshipped as Gauri.
Warrior goddess; slays the buffalo demon Mahishasura; depicted with ten arms, riding a lion. Her ten-day festival is celebrated as Navaratri, ending in Vijayadashami.
Six-headed son of Shiva and Parvati; god of war; also called Murugan in the Tamil tradition; Skanda in the Sanskritic.
In the Mahabharata, eldest son of Kunti — born of the sun-god Surya before her marriage; raised by a charioteer family; sworn ally of Duryodhana; killed by Arjuna at Kurukshetra.
Tribal prince in the Mahabharata; learned archery before a clay idol of Drona, who later asked for his right thumb as guru-dakshina to ensure Arjuna's primacy.

Son of Arjuna and Subhadra in the Mahabharata; killed at age 16 on the 13th day of Kurukshetra after entering the Chakravyuha — the rotating military formation he had only learned how to enter, not how to exit.
Common wife of the five Pandavas in the Mahabharata; daughter of King Drupada; born of fire from the yagna fire-pit; also called Panchali and Krishnaa.
24th and last of the Jain Tirthankaras; born around 599 BCE in Bihar; gave Jainism its modern philosophical form. Birth name Vardhamana.
Punjabi Hindi-cinema playback singer (1924-1980); the dominant male voice of the 1950s-70s; over 7,000 songs; Padma Shri 1967.
Hindi-cinema playback singer (1923-76); the singing voice for Raj Kapoor; songs like 'Mera Joota Hai Japani' and 'Awara Hoon'.

Bengali-Hindi playback singer (1929-87); from Khandwa, MP; younger brother of Ashok Kumar; sang 'Mere Sapnon Ki Rani', 'Roop Tera Mastana', and his own 'Aane Wala Pal'. Also acted, directed, produced.
Bengali playback singer (1919-2013) with strong classical Hindustani training; songs like 'Lagi Tumse Mann Ki Lagan' and 'Pucho Na Kaise Maine Rain Bitayi'.
Lucknow-born playback singer (1924-1998), known for the slight tremor in his voice; songs like 'Jalte Hain Jiske Liye' and 'Hum Pyar Mein Jalne Walon Ko'. The 'King of Ghazal' before Jagjit Singh.
Hindustani classical and ghazal vocalist (1914-74); 'Mallika-e-Ghazal'; born Akhtari Bai in Faizabad, UP; Padma Bhushan 1968.
Hindustani classical vocalist of the Jaipur-Atrauli gharana; her 1953 recording of 'Jaat Kahan Ho' was selected by Carl Sagan to fly aboard NASA's Voyager Golden Record into deep space.
Bansuri (bamboo flute) maestro; Padma Vibhushan; played for Yash Chopra's 'Silsila' and 'Lamhe' soundtracks alongside Shiv Kumar Sharma — together credited as Shiv-Hari.
Shehnai maestro from Varanasi (1916-2006); played the shehnai at the Red Fort on the night of 15 August 1947 to mark India's independence; Bharat Ratna 2001.
Hindustani classical vocalist of the Mewati gharana (1930-2020); known for singing the rare 'morning' raga 'Haveli Sangeet'; Padma Vibhushan 2000.
Indian writer best known for popular fiction targeting young Indians; his debut, 'Five Point Someone' (2004), was loosely adapted as '3 Idiots'; later wrote 'Two States' and 'Half Girlfriend'.
Indian-American author; won the Pulitzer for Fiction in 2000 for her debut short-story collection 'Interpreter of Maladies'. Born in London, raised in Rhode Island.
Indian English novelist of the 1930s; his 'Untouchable' (1935) follows a single day in the life of a Dalit sweeper, Bakha; one of the founders of Indian English fiction.
Karnataka-born Indian English novelist; his 'Kanthapura' (1938) is set in a Mysore village's Gandhian awakening; later 'The Serpent and the Rope'. Sahitya Akademi Fellow.
Bengal-born novelist who wrote in English; 'Clear Light of Day', 'In Custody', 'Fasting Feasting'; Booker shortlist three times. Mother of a more recent Booker winner.

Indian politician, diplomat, and author of 'The Great Indian Novel' (1989), 'An Era of Darkness' (2016) and 'Why I Am a Hindu' (2018). Trinity College, Cambridge; UN; Lok Sabha MP for Thiruvananthapuram.
Hindi-Urdu novelist (1880-1936); pen name meaning 'moon of love'; novels like 'Godaan' (1936), 'Karmabhoomi' and 'Rangbhoomi' shaped modern Hindi prose.
Urdu short-story writer (1912-55); his Partition stories, especially 'Toba Tek Singh', remain among the most-cited literary responses to 1947. Migrated to Lahore in 1948.
Urdu writer (1915-91); her 1942 short story 'Lihaaf' (The Quilt) was tried for obscenity in a Lahore court; remembered as a fearless feminist voice in mid-century Indian literature.
Bengali writer and activist (1926-2016); 'Hajar Churashir Ma' (Mother of 1084) and 'Aranyer Adhikar' confronted the Naxalite era and tribal land rights; Jnanpith Award 1996.
Kannada novelist (1932-2014); his 1965 novel 'Samskara' (rendered into a landmark film by Pattabhirama Reddy) is one of modern Indian literature's defining works; Jnanpith 1994.
Urdu poet (1877-1938); his 'Sare Jahan Se Achha Hindostan Hamara' (1904) is sung as a patriotic anthem in India; later wrote 'Bang-i-Dara' and articulated the idea of a separate Muslim state.
Father of the Indian nuclear programme; founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in 1945; died in a plane crash on Mont Blanc in January 1966.
Father of the Indian space programme; founder of the Physical Research Laboratory at Ahmedabad and of ISRO; died unexpectedly at Kovalam in December 1971.
Tamil-born physicist; Nobel Prize for Physics 1930 for his discovery, while at Calcutta in 1928, that light scattered by a transparent material changes wavelength. The phenomenon bears his name.
Bengali polymath; pioneered research on plant physiology and demonstrated that plants respond to stimuli; invented the crescograph; founded the Bose Institute at Calcutta in 1917. Initials J.C.
Punjab-born molecular biologist; shared the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine 1968 for deciphering the genetic code and its function in protein synthesis.
Astrophysicist; Nobel Prize for Physics 1983 for his theoretical work on the structure and evolution of stars; the limit of stable mass for a white dwarf carries his name.
Mumbai-born ornithologist (1896-1987); the 'Birdman of India'; surveyed birds of every region from Kashmir to Kerala; the bird sanctuary at Bharatpur is now named after him.
First Field Marshal of India (1973); Indian Army Chief during the 1971 war that led to the creation of Bangladesh; born in Amritsar in 1914 to a Parsi family.
Mysore-born civil engineer and statesman; Diwan of Mysore (1912-18); designed the Krishna Raja Sagara dam; his birthday, 15 September, is celebrated as Engineer's Day in India. Bharat Ratna 1955.
Garhwali environmentalist who, in the 1970s, led the Chipko movement — villagers hugging trees to prevent logging contractors from felling them. Indian-government honour Padma Vibhushan 2009.
Kerala-born track athlete; the 'Payyoli Express'; missed an Olympic 400m hurdles bronze at Los Angeles 1984 by one-hundredth of a second. Initials P.T.

He scored a hat-trick in the gold-medal match of the 1936 Berlin Olympics, where India crushed Germany 8-1; said to have refused offers from Hitler to join the German army; his birthday, 29 August, is India's National Sports Day.
Andhra-born weightlifter; first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal — bronze in the 69 kg category at Sydney 2000. Padma Shri.
UP-born Indian fast bowler with a textbook seam-up action; took 7 wickets for 57 against New Zealand in the 2023 ODI World Cup semi-final at the Wankhede.
Saurashtra-born Test specialist; the man who blunted Australia's attack at Sydney in January 2021 (50 in the second innings, taking 11 blows to the body); Dravid's natural successor at number three.
Captained India to a famous Test series win at the Gabba in January 2021 in the absence of Virat Kohli; Mumbai middle-order batter; nicknamed 'Jinks'.
Roorkee-born wicketkeeper-batter; his unbeaten 89 chased down 328 at the Gabba in January 2021, ending Australia's 32-year unbeaten home run there. Aggressive left-hander.
Punjab-born young Indian opener; double century against New Zealand in 2024; nicknamed 'Prince' for his classical technique.
Baroda-born Indian all-rounder; T20 captain; younger brother of an India spinner; comeback hero of the 2022 Asia Cup. Initials H.P.
UP-born India seamer; specialist swing bowler; took 5/19 against Australia in his first ODI series in 2013-14. Initials B.K.
Punjab-born all-rounder; first Indian to score a Test century, hitting 118 against England at Bombay in December 1933 on his debut. Later India's first Test captain post-independence.
Maharashtra batter; led India in their first ever Test win — against England at Madras in February 1952; the country's third Test captain. The Vijay Hazare Trophy is named after him.

Bombay opener of the 1930s and 40s; first-class average of 71.64, second only to Bradman among all batsmen with 50+ first-class innings; never went on a Test tour because of cricket-board politics for much of his career.
Cricketing nawab who played 3 Tests for England in the 1932-34 Bodyline series, then captained India in 1946. His son later captained India for far longer.
Punjab-born swing bowler; opening bowler in the 1983 World Cup final at Lord's, where he dismissed Gordon Greenidge with the very first ball of the West Indies innings. Initials B.S.
Goa-born middle-order batter; 642 runs in the 1970-71 series in the West Indies — the 'Renaissance' of Indian cricket — including 212 at Kingston, 112 at Port of Spain, and 150 at Bridgetown.

Pioneer of women's cricket in India; left-arm spinner; captained the side in the 1970s and 80s; over 100 wickets in Tests and ODIs combined; later a member of the Committee of Administrators that ran the BCCI.
Punjab-born middle-order batter; scored a vital 61 in the 1983 World Cup semi-final at Old Trafford against England, taking India to the final.
The 'Showman' of Indian cinema; born 1924; founded RK Films; made 'Awara' (1951), 'Shree 420' (1955), 'Mera Naam Joker' (1970), 'Bobby' (1973). Father of Rishi, grandfather of Ranbir.
'Evergreen' Hindi film actor (1923-2011); brother of Vijay (Goldie) and Chetan; films include 'Guide' (1965), 'Jewel Thief' (1967), 'Hare Rama Hare Krishna' (1971); founded Navketan Films.
Mumbai-born actor (1965-); the 'perfectionist'; 'Lagaan' (2001), '3 Idiots' (2009), 'PK' (2014), 'Dangal' (2016).
Mumbai-born actor (1965-); the 'Bhaijaan' of Bollywood; films include 'Maine Pyar Kiya' (1989), 'Hum Aapke Hain Koun' (1994), 'Dabangg' (2010), 'Sultan' (2016).

Director and producer; runs Dharma Productions (founded by his father Yash Johar); directed 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' (1998), 'Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham' (2001), 'My Name is Khan' (2010); chat show 'Koffee with...' him.
Mumbai-born director; films include 'Munna Bhai MBBS' (2003), 'Lage Raho Munna Bhai' (2006), '3 Idiots' (2009) and 'PK' (2014). All starring Aamir or Sanjay Dutt.
Ayodhya-born actress; 'Rab Ne Bana Di Jodi' (2008) was her debut opposite Shah Rukh Khan; later 'PK', 'Sultan'; founded Clean Slate Filmz; married Virat Kohli in 2017.
Bengaluru-born actress, Konkani by background; daughter of Indian badminton player Prakash Padukone; 'Om Shanti Om' (2007), 'Cocktail' (2012), 'Padmaavat' (2018).

Born Fatima Rashid in Calcutta in 1929; she played the long-suffering peasant matriarch in 'Mother India' (1957); married her co-star and director Sunil Dutt-collaboration partner of the same film. Padma Shri 1958.
Born Mahjabeen Bano in 1933; the 'Tragedy Queen' of Hindi cinema; iconic in 'Pakeezah' (released in 1972, two months before her death), 'Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam' (1962).
Bengaluru-born Hindi cinema actress (1938-2023); 'Pyaasa' (1957), 'Kaagaz Ke Phool' (1959), 'Guide' (1965), 'Khamoshi' (1969); muse of Guru Dutt; Padma Shri 1972, Padma Bhushan 2011.
Hindi cinema actress (1936-91); 'Bandini' (1963), 'Sujata' (1959), 'Bandini' won her the Filmfare; mother of actor Mohnish Bahl; never made a sequel film. Single-name screen identity.
Hindi cinema actor known as 'Bharat' for the patriotic roles he played and directed: 'Upkar' (1967), 'Purab Aur Paschim' (1970), 'Roti Kapda Aur Makaan' (1974), 'Kranti' (1981).
Bengali director (1909-66); 'Do Bigha Zamin' (1953), 'Devdas' (1955), 'Madhumati' (1958); brought Bengali realism to Hindi cinema; mentor to Hrishikesh Mukherjee.
Bengali director (1922-2006); 'Anand' (1971), 'Bawarchi' (1972), 'Gol Maal' (1979), 'Chupke Chupke' (1975); the gentle, middle-class chronicler of Hindi cinema.
Director of intimate Mumbai middle-class comedies; 'Chhoti Si Baat' (1976), 'Rajnigandha' (1974), 'Baton Baton Mein' (1979); not to be confused with the Bengali Ray.
Marathi-Hindi director; 'Sant Tukaram' (1937), 'Do Aankhen Barah Haath' (1957) which won the Golden Globe; founded Prabhat Film Company; the 'V' before his single-name surname.
Independent-cinema director; 'Black Friday' (2004), 'Gangs of Wasseypur' (2012), 'Ugly' (2013); also a producer who launched many other directors. UP-born.
Indian Brahmin scholar and royal advisor (4th c BCE); composed the 'Arthashastra', the great treatise on statecraft; mentor to Chandragupta Maurya. Two names, both well-known.
Founder of the Mauryan Empire (322 BCE), with Chanakya's guidance; capital at Pataliputra; ended the Nanda dynasty.
Mauryan emperor (3rd c BCE); after the bloody Kalinga War, he embraced Buddhism and propagated dharma through edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars across the subcontinent.
The bloody battle of 261 BCE in modern Odisha that horrified Ashoka into embracing Buddhism. The kingdom that Ashoka conquered, name?
Akbar's chief witty courtier, his 'Birbal'-real-name was Mahesh Das; one of Akbar's nine 'Navaratnas'. Most folktales of Akbar's court name him alongside the emperor.
Akbar's court musician; one of the Navaratnas; ascribed with composing the ragas Miyan ki Todi and Miyan Malhar; born Tanna Mishra near Gwalior.
Group of Hindu and Jain temples in Madhya Pradesh built by the Chandela dynasty between roughly 950 and 1050 CE; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986; famed for their erotic sculptures.
Sun Temple in Odisha, built in the mid-13th century by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty; designed as a giant chariot of Surya with 12 pairs of stone wheels.
Group of about 30 Buddhist rock-cut cave monuments in Maharashtra, dating from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE; rediscovered by a British officer hunting tigers in 1819.
Cave complex near Aurangabad in Maharashtra with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain rock-cut temples side by side; the Hindu Kailasa temple in Cave 16 was carved top-down out of a single rock.

On 23 January 1565, an alliance of Deccan sultanates decisively defeated the Vijayanagara Empire under Aliya Rama Raya at this battlefield in northern Karnataka. Rama Raya was killed and Hampi sacked.
Sultan of Delhi from 1211 to 1236; son-in-law of Qutbuddin Aibak; completed construction of the Qutub Minar; established the Delhi Sultanate's foundations.

Khilji-dynasty Sultan of Delhi (r. 1296-1316); pushed Sultanate boundaries deep into the Deccan via his general Malik Kafur; instituted famous market-price reforms; obsessed in legend with the Rajput queen Padmini.
Tughlaq Sultan of Delhi (r. 1325-51); famously moved the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan and back; introduced token currency that collapsed; Ibn Battuta visited his court.

5th-century Indian astronomer and mathematician; in his work 'Aryabhatiya' (499 CE), he proposed that the earth rotates on its axis and gave a remarkably accurate value for pi. India's first satellite was named after him.
7th-century mathematician and astronomer from western India; his 'Brahmasphutasiddhanta' contains the first known explicit treatment of zero as a number, with rules for arithmetic involving it.
12th-century Karnataka mathematician; his 'Lilavati' is a treatise on arithmetic in verse, written for and named after his daughter; also gave an early statement of differential calculus concepts.
7th-century Sanskrit court poet of Emperor Harsha; wrote the biographical 'Harshacharita' and the romance 'Kadambari' — among the earliest surviving Sanskrit prose narratives.

King of the Pushyabhuti dynasty (r. 606-647); ruled much of north India from Kanauj; the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited his court; often called the last great pre-medieval Hindu emperor of north India.
4th-century Gupta emperor (c. 335-380 CE); his Allahabad Pillar inscription, composed by his court poet Harishena, lists his many conquests; sometimes called the 'Indian Napoleon'.
Mountain range stretching across Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi — geologically among the oldest in the world; Mt Abu and Guru Shikhar are its highest points.
Mountain range running roughly east-west across central India, traditionally taken as the dividing line between North and South India.
Mountain range north of the western Himalayas, where K2 — the world's second-highest peak, at 8,611 m — is located. Spread across India, Pakistan and China.
182-metre statue of Sardar Patel inaugurated in October 2018 on an island in the Narmada near the Sardar Sarovar Dam in Gujarat — the world's tallest statue at the time of its unveiling.
The four sacred Hindu pilgrimage sites in Uttarakhand: Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath. Collective name (two Hindi words).
First national park established in India (1936); in Uttarakhand; named after a British hunter-turned-conservationist who chronicled man-eating tigers in the Kumaon hills.
Assam national park along the Brahmaputra; UNESCO site; home to roughly two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinoceroses.
Tiger reserve in Kerala, around an artificial lake; tiger and elephant habitat; named after the river that flows through it.
High-altitude pass in Ladakh, long claimed (with some dispute) as the world's highest motorable pass; gateway to the Nubra Valley.
Strategic high-altitude pass on the Srinagar-Leh highway; closed by snow for much of the winter; connects Kashmir to Ladakh.
Border crossing between India and Pakistan, near Amritsar; site of the daily flag-lowering retreat ceremony watched by spectators on both sides.
Lake in the heart of Srinagar in Jammu & Kashmir; famed for its houseboats, shikaras and floating gardens.
Largest inland salt lake in India, in Rajasthan; produces about 9 percent of the country's salt; a Ramsar wetland and a haven for flamingos.
UNESCO World Heritage ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire's capital, on the banks of the Tungabhadra in Karnataka; spread across boulder-strewn landscape; sacked in 1565.
UNESCO site near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh; rock shelters with prehistoric paintings dating back perhaps 30,000 years; one of the oldest evidence of human settlement in India.
UNESCO Buddhist monument in Madhya Pradesh; the Great Stupa was originally commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE; gateways carved with Jataka tales.
Tamil Nadu coastal town with a UNESCO group of Pallava-era rock-cut and structural temples, including the Shore Temple and the Five Rathas.
Bihar town where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment under a pipal tree; the Mahabodhi Temple here is a UNESCO site.
India's central bank; established in April 1935 under the RBI Act 1934; nationalised in 1949; headquartered in Mumbai.
Largest public-sector bank in India; formed in 1955 as the successor to the Imperial Bank of India; majority-owned by the Government of India. Three letters.
Ahmedabad-based Indian conglomerate founded in 1988 by a Gujarati commodities trader; today spans ports, energy, airports, cement and media; the founder's name lends itself to the group.
Founder of Sun Pharmaceuticals, India's largest pharma company; born in Amreli, Gujarat; Padma Shri 2016.
Founder and chairman of Bharti Airtel; among the architects of India's telecom revolution from the mid-1990s onwards. Padma Bhushan 2007.

Mumbai-born industrialist; succeeded Ratan Tata as chairman of Tata Sons in 2012; ousted by the board in October 2016 in a public corporate-governance row; died in a road accident on the Mumbai-Ahmedabad highway in September 2022.
Indian-American economist; Governor of the Reserve Bank of India 2013-16; chief economist of the IMF before that; predicted the 2008 financial crisis at a famous Jackson Hole talk in 2005.
IAS officer who has served as Governor of the Reserve Bank of India since December 2018; previously Economic Affairs Secretary; oversaw demonetisation's aftermath.
Founder of the Sahara India Pariwar; in 2014 was sent to Tihar Jail in a long-running case involving non-refundable bond schemes; died in November 2023.
Karnataka entrepreneur; founder of Café Coffee Day, the chain that effectively introduced coffee-shop culture to urban India; ended his own life in July 2019. Initials V.G.

Diamond merchant who, with his uncle Mehul Choksi, was at the centre of a roughly fourteen-thousand-crore-rupee fraud against Punjab National Bank that broke in February 2018; subsequently fled India and was arrested in London.
Third-generation chairman of the Aditya Birla Group; took charge in 1995 after the early death of his father Aditya Birla; the AV Birla cement-and-aluminium-and-telecom empire under his stewardship.

Constitutional amendment that — rolled out from 1 July 2017 — implemented a unified national tax across the country, subsuming a thicket of state and central indirect taxes. Three-letter abbreviation.
Indian central act passed in 2005, giving citizens the legal right to demand information from any public authority within 30 days. Three-letter abbreviation.

1979 commission set up under the Janata government to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes; its 1980 report recommended 27% reservations for OBCs in central government jobs and education.
Indian statutory body, established in 2010 under an Act of Parliament, to deal with cases involving the environment, forests and biodiversity. Three-letter abbreviation.
Replaced the Planning Commission of India in January 2015; its name is also the Sanskrit word for 'policy'.
Article of the Indian Constitution that, until its abrogation in August 2019, gave special autonomous status to Jammu & Kashmir.
Kerala-born jurist; first woman judge of the Supreme Court of India, appointed in 1989; later Governor of Tamil Nadu.
First woman Chief Justice of any Indian High Court (Himachal Pradesh, 1991); also one of the first three women to be made an Indian High Court judge; mother of writer Vikram Seth.

2005 committee set up by PM Manmohan Singh to study the social, economic and educational status of India's Muslim community; its 2006 report had a marked impact on minority-welfare policy. Named after its chair.

1932 agreement between Gandhi and Ambedkar at Yerwada Jail, Pune, which abandoned the British proposal of separate electorates for Depressed Classes in favour of joint electorates with reserved seats. Two-word name.
Last major British constitutional reform for India before independence; introduced provincial autonomy and a federal structure that the 1950 Constitution drew heavily on.

1946 British delegation led by Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander, sent to India to negotiate transfer of power; rejected the demand for Pakistan but proposed a three-tier structure.
Younger brother of Rama; accompanies him into exile; husband of Urmila; in the Lanka war, falls grievously wounded and is revived only when Hanuman fetches the Sanjeevani herb.
Brother of Rama; rules Ayodhya in his absence by placing Rama's sandals on the throne; refuses the throne to which his mother Kaikeyi tried to elevate him.
Wife of Rama in the Ramayana; said to have been born from a furrow in the earth, found by King Janaka of Mithila; abducted by Ravana and finally returns to the earth from which she came.
Vanara king allied with Rama in the Ramayana, after Rama helps him reclaim his throne from his brother Vali. He sends Hanuman to find Sita.
Second of the five Pandava brothers in the Mahabharata; said to be the strongest, son of the wind-god Vayu; kills Duryodhana in single combat at Kurukshetra.
Third of the five Pandavas; the great archer of the Mahabharata; recipient of the Bhagavad Gita; son of Indra and Kunti.

Son of Drona in the Mahabharata; born with a divine gem on his forehead; the cursed warrior who unleashes the Brahmastra at the end of Kurukshetra and is condemned by Krishna to wander the earth, immortal but in agony.
General of King Virata in the Mahabharata; harasses Draupadi during the Pandavas' year of incognito service in Virata's court; killed by Bhima at her instigation.
Hindus traditionally count four Vedas. Name any one. (Hint: one is associated with hymns, one with melody, one with sacrificial formulae, and one with charms.)
Andhra Pradesh hill shrine; one of the world's most-visited and richest pilgrimage sites; the deity is Lord Venkateswara, a form of Vishnu.

Odisha temple town whose annual Rath Yatra in the month of Asadha sees three deities — the lord of the universe, his sister and his elder brother — pulled out in colossal wooden chariots through the streets.
8th-century Kerala-born philosopher; expounder of Advaita Vedanta; established the four mathas at Sringeri, Puri, Dwarka and Jyotirmath; commentary on the Brahmasutras and the principal Upanishads.

Sarod maestro (1922-2009); son and student of Allauddin Khan; widely regarded as one of the foremost classical musicians of the 20th century; received the Padma Vibhushan and a National Heritage Fellowship.
Sitar maestro of the Imdadkhani gharana (1928-2004); long-time rival of Pandit Ravi Shankar; refused to accept the Padma awards he was offered, wanting only the Bharat Ratna.
Sarod player of the Senia Bangash gharana, born in Gwalior in 1945; trained by his father Hafiz Ali Khan; Padma Vibhushan 2001.

Jammu-born santoor maestro (1938-2022); transformed a Kashmiri folk instrument into a Hindustani classical solo instrument; collaborated with Hariprasad Chaurasia on Yash Chopra film soundtracks under the name 'Shiv-Hari'.
Pakistani ghazal maestro (1940-); 'Chupke Chupke Raat Din', 'Hungama Hai Kyon Barpa'; immensely popular on both sides of the border.
Punjabi Urdu poet and Hindi-cinema lyricist (1921-80); his lyrics for 'Pyaasa' (1957), 'Phir Subah Hogi' (1958), 'Hum Dono' (1961) and 'Kabhi Kabhie' (1976) are landmarks of Hindi film poetry.
One of the three composers of the 'Trinity' of Carnatic music (alongside Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri); a Telugu Brahmin, lived 1767-1847; thousands of his kritis are still sung today.
Punjabi-Bengali singer-actor (1904-47); the first major star of Indian playback; songs like 'Babul Mora Naihar Chuto Jaye' from 'Street Singer' (1938); died at 42 from alcoholism.
Bengali playback singer and composer (1905-78); contemporary of Saigal at New Theatres in Calcutta; composed and sang for many of the early 1930s talkies.
Mumbai-based ghazal and playback singer; collaborator with Lesle Lewis on the duo 'Colonial Cousins' in the mid-1990s; Padma Shri 2004.
Rajasthan-born ghazal singer (1941-2011); 'Hothon Se Choo Lo Tum', 'Tum Itna Jo Muskura Rahe Ho', 'Chitthi Na Koi Sandesh'; arguably the singer who took the ghazal mainstream in India.
Assamese poet, lyricist, music director and singer (1926-2011); composed and sang 'Dil Hoom Hoom Kare' for 'Rudaali' (1993); Bharat Ratna posthumously in 2019.
Author of 'Sacred Games' (2006), the sprawling Bombay underworld novel later adapted by Netflix as the streaming service's first Indian original. Brother of the writer-filmmaker Anuradha.
Parsi-Canadian novelist born in Bombay in 1952; 'Such a Long Journey' (1991), 'A Fine Balance' (1995), 'Family Matters' (2002) — all Booker-shortlisted.
Indian historian and writer; 'A Corner of a Foreign Field' (cricket), 'India After Gandhi' (2007), 'Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World'; also a one-time Wisden columnist.
Indian essayist and intellectual historian; 'From the Ruins of Empire' (2012), 'Age of Anger' (2017), 'Bland Fanatics' (2020).
Indian-British novelist and travel writer; 'Stranger to History: A Son's Journey through Islamic Lands' (2009); son of the Pakistani politician Salman Taseer.

Mughal-era Urdu and Persian poet (1797-1869); his ghazals — 'Hazaaron Khwahishein Aisi', 'Dil-e-Nadan Tujhe Hua Kya Hai' — remain a high-water mark of Urdu poetry; lived through the 1857 Revolt in Old Delhi.
Pakistani Urdu poet of resistance (1911-84); 'Hum Dekhenge', 'Mujhse Pehli Si Mohabbat Mere Mehboob Na Mang'; spent years in exile from Zia-ul-Haq's Pakistan.
15th-century mystic poet of the Bhakti movement, who composed couplets ('dohas') in vernacular Hindi sceptical of caste, ritualism and orthodoxy in both Hinduism and Islam.
16th-century Awadhi poet who composed the 'Ramcharitmanas', a retelling of the Ramayana that became the most widely-read religious text of north India.
Rajput princess turned 16th-century Bhakti poet; her bhajans — sung in praise of Krishna as her beloved — are still performed widely; she renounced palace life and wandered as a saint-poet.
Tamil poet (1882-1921) and freedom-movement activist; his patriotic and devotional verses redefined modern Tamil poetry; honorific 'Mahakavi'.
Malayalam-English poet and writer (1934-2009); 'My Story' (1976) was a frank autobiography; her poems in English — 'An Introduction', 'The Old Playhouse' — were widely anthologised.
Calcutta-born athlete who won two silver medals at the 1900 Paris Olympics — in the 200m and the 200m hurdles — and is officially listed by the IOC as India's first Olympic medallist.
Maharashtra-born wrestler; bronze in bantamweight wrestling at the Helsinki 1952 Olympics — the first individual Olympic medal for independent India.
Indian tennis player; won an Olympic bronze in men's singles at Atlanta 1996 — at the time, India's first individual medal in 44 years; later a doubles Grand Slam champion.
Haryana-born wrestler; bronze at Beijing 2008, silver at London 2012 — making him, at the time, the most successful Indian individual Olympian. Two-time world champion.
Hisar-born badminton player; bronze at London 2012 — first Indian to win an Olympic medal in badminton; once world No. 1.
Hyderabad-born badminton player; won silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020; protégée of Pullela Gopichand.
Manipuri weightlifter; silver in the 49 kg category at Tokyo 2020 — India's first medal of those games. Padma Shri 2018.
Haryana-born javelin thrower; gold at Tokyo 2020 with a throw of 87.58 m — India's first individual track-and-field Olympic gold.

Hyderabad-born tennis player; first Indian woman to win a Grand Slam title — the 2009 Australian Open mixed doubles, partnered with Mahesh Bhupathi; later a multiple women's doubles Grand Slam champion.
Albanian-born Roman Catholic nun who lived in Calcutta from 1929; founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950; Nobel Peace Prize 1979; canonised in 2016.
Bengali-born economist; born 1933 at Santiniketan; Nobel Prize in Economics 1998 for contributions to welfare economics, social choice theory, and the study of famines (notably Bengal, 1943).
MIT economist born in Kolkata in 1961; shared the Nobel Prize in Economics 2019 with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.
Tamil-born structural biologist based in Cambridge; shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009 for his work on the structure and function of the ribosome.
Indian children's-rights campaigner; founded the Bachpan Bachao Andolan in 1980; shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 with Malala Yousafzai.

Kerala-born botanist (1897-1984); the first Indian woman to receive a PhD in botany from a US university; her cytogenetic work on sugarcane led to high-yielding hybrid varieties widely planted in India.

Bengali organic chemist (1917-2006); the first woman to be awarded the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize for science (1961); her work on vinca alkaloids and antimalarials shaped Indian pharmaceutical research.
Punjab-born hockey forward (1924-2020); scored five of India's six goals in the 1952 Olympic hockey final at Helsinki against the Netherlands; three-time Olympic gold medallist (1948, 1952, 1956).
Kerala-born hockey goalkeeper; instrumental in India's bronze medals at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024; nicknamed 'The Wall' for goalkeepers. Initials P.R.
Indian football team captain since 2012; born in Secunderabad in 1984; over 90 international goals — among the most ever for any active player. Surname?
Connect: Lata Mangeshkar, Sachin Tendulkar, APJ Abdul Kalam, Ustad Bismillah Khan.
questions.explanation: All four were awarded India's highest civilian honour.

questions.question: Connect: Rabindranath Tagore, CV Raman, Mother Teresa, Amartya Sen, Hargobind Khorana.
questions.explanation: All Indian or Indian-origin Nobel laureates: Tagore (Literature 1913), Raman (Physics 1930), Mother Teresa (Peace 1979), Sen (Economics 1998), Khorana (Medicine 1968).

questions.question: Connect: 1526, 1556, 1761. All three years saw a decisive battle on the same Haryana field. The field?
questions.explanation: The First (Babur vs Lodi), Second (Akbar's forces vs Hemu) and Third (Marathas vs Abdali) Battles of Panipat.

questions.question: What ties Hampi, Mahabalipuram, Khajuraho, Sanchi, the Sun Temple at Konark and the Ajanta Caves?
questions.explanation: All six are UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India.

questions.question: Connect: Indira Gandhi (1984), Rajiv Gandhi (1991), Mahatma Gandhi (1948).
questions.explanation: All three were assassinated; the years are the years of their deaths.

questions.question: Connect: Pandit Ravi Shankar, Rishikesh, Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, the Beatles' 1968 visit.
questions.explanation: All four are nodes of the Beatles' Indian-music-and-meditation phase, which crystallised in their 1968 stay at the Maharishi's ashram in Rishikesh.

questions.question: Connect: Andhra Pradesh (1953), Maharashtra (1960), Gujarat (1960), Haryana (1966), Telangana (2014).
questions.answer: Indian states formed by linguistic or political reorganisation
questions.explanation: Each was carved out of a larger state — usually on linguistic grounds, sometimes (Telangana, Haryana) on a mix of regional and political grounds.

questions.question: Connect: Sarojini Naidu (Congress, 1925), Indira Gandhi (Prime Minister, 1966), M Fathima Beevi (Supreme Court, 1989), Pratibha Patil (President, 2007).
questions.answer: First Indian women in their respective offices
accept: first women to hold these offices
first indian women in their offices
questions.explanation: Each was the first Indian woman to hold the office mentioned.

questions.question: Connect: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Syama Sastri.
questions.explanation: The three composer-saints of 18th-century Tanjore who together shaped modern Carnatic music.

questions.question: Connect: Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev Thapar, Shivaram Rajguru — all hanged on a single date in March 1931.
questions.explanation: All three were hanged at Lahore Central Jail on the evening of 23 March 1931 in the Lahore Conspiracy Case — now observed as Shaheed Diwas (Martyrs' Day).

questions.question: Connect: KD Jadhav (Helsinki 1952, bronze), Abhinav Bindra (Beijing 2008, gold), Karnam Malleswari (Sydney 2000, bronze), Neeraj Chopra (Tokyo 2020, gold).
questions.explanation: Each was a milestone individual Olympic medal for independent India — Jadhav the first, Malleswari the first by an Indian woman, Bindra the first individual gold, Chopra the first track-and-field gold.

questions.question: Connect: Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Bhaskara II.
questions.explanation: All three were great mathematician-astronomers of classical India — 5th, 7th and 12th centuries respectively — whose work on astronomy, zero and algebra shaped the field.
